name: Armenian
confidence_why: Dum-Tragut 2009, Vaux 1994/1998, Dolatian, Sharifzadeh and Vaux 2023 and the instrumental studies of Chakmakjian, Dolatian and Skopeteas 2024 and Seyfarth et al. 2024 all put Standard Eastern Armenian main stress on the final syllable (the last non-schwa vowel), and the one dissenter, Haghverdi 2016, a one-speaker MA thesis, argues that stress is final even before a schwa, which questions the schwa exception but not the final placement.

catalog_quote: In Modern Eastern Armenian, the stress lies on the last syllable with a full vowel-nucleus. The stressed vowel is characterised by greater loudness, higher pitch and (in general) greater lengths. Some examples: girk' "book", grk'í "book, DAT", grk'ér "books", ěnkér "friend", ěnkrój "friend, DAT", ěnkernér "friends" ... In some cases, the stress lies on the penultimate syllable: – If the vowel contained in the last closed syllable is the schwa [ə], as in káysr, ástł – In some words, the stress is on the penultimate rather than on the last syllable, e.g. órewě "any", núynisk "even" ... – If the last consonant of a word is represented by a definite article-suffix -ě, or -n, possessive suffix -s-, -d, e.g. całíkě [tsałíkə] "the flower" ... sweep_summary: Two title-hits for Eastern Armenian, neither obtainable. (1) Skopeteas 2021 is an unpublished Bielefeld/Göttingen manuscript on focus and question intonation (prosody, not stress placement); no copy exists in any index or repository reached, and its content is known only second-hand through Seyfarth et al. 2024 (JIPA, held by the project) and its published successor Chakmakjian, Dolatian & Skopeteas 2024 (Speech Prosody, held by the project, 'confirms'). (2) Dolatian 2021a (NLLT 39: 843-886) is closed access; Springer serves only a preview (abstract silent on stress placement; a footnote mentions that high vowels lack secondary stress), and Springer's PDF is blocked by a JS challenge; no repository copy. this search of works with stress in the title did yield one new open first-hand statement, from the Glossa article that cites both items: Dolatian 2022 (Glossa 7(1), p. 7), 'Stress is on the rightmost non-schwa vowel in the prosodic word (Vaux 1998; Dolatian 2021a)', which confirms the catalog's fixed-strict coding but does not supersede Dum-Tragut 2009 (or the already-held Seyfarth et al. 2024 description).

new_statements.quote: Many descriptions of Eastern Armenian (EA) agree that word stress lies on the final syllable unless it contains a schwa, in which case stress retracts to the penult (Khachatryan 1988, Vaux 1998, Dum-Tragut 2009). [...] Instead, EA is analyzed most accurately as exhibiting a uniformly final metrical head. [p. 1] [...] This paper has shown that Eastern Armenian stress is consistently final in the PrWd. This finding contrasts with previous grammatical descriptions as having a stress system conditioned by the presence or lack of schwa in the final syllable of a word. [...] acoustic data corroborates a Final Stress Hypothesis whereby accent is placed on the final vowel, without regard for its sonority or quality. [p. 33]

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog's plain fixed: final syllable code (Gordon stress placement coded per word length as 11 101 1001 (1 = a stressed syllable)) and in fact strengthens it (final even before schwa), but explicitly contradicts the schwa clause of the existing statement (Dolatian 2022 / Vaux 1998: 'stress is on the rightmost non-schwa vowel'): for CV(C)CəC words Dolatian/Vaux put stress on the penult full vowel, Haghverdi's acoustic data put the LH* head on the final schwa. It also questions the type: the prominence may be a pitch accent (LH*) rather than stress. Evidence is from one speaker of standard Eastern Armenian.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word-level prominence in Eastern Armenian falls on the final syllable of the prosodic word, including when that syllable's vowel is schwa; the thesis rejects the received 'final full vowel, retract to penult before schwa' rule. Phonetically the only consistent correlate found (one native speaker, disyllabic CVCVC / CVCəC targets in focused and unfocused frames) was an LH* pitch rise on the final syllable; duration, intensity and vowel quality did not distinguish putative heads from non-heads. The abstract (p. iii) adds that the result 'casts doubt on impressionistic reports of stress, which are possibly tonal or pitch accent systems', and sec. 4 (p. 30) leaves open whether the final LH is a word-boundary tone rather than metrical structure at all.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not measured. p. 5 mentions initial secondary stress only hypothetically ('Even if the initial syllable in such words had secondary stress, schwa is clearly not banned under secondary stress because CəCVCV is a perfectly acceptable word').
new_statements.exceptions: The definite -ə and possessive -s/-t (with epenthetic ə) are suggested to be clitics that may lie outside the prosodic word, which would explain earlier 'penult' impressions for schwa-final words (pp. 6, 29); onomatopoeic forms allow consecutive schwas (p. 5 fn. 2); high-vowel reduction/deletion patterns discussed in sec. 2 are reanalysed as phonotactic (ban on consecutive schwas), not stress-driven; results are from a single speaker, two further participants not yet analysed (p. 30); disyllabic targets only (p. 31).
new_statements.identity_note: Haghverdi 2016 describes standard Eastern Armenian (data from a single native speaker); the listing's 'Vahagn.. Ph.D. dissertation' is wrong: title page reads Vartan Haghverdi, Master of Arts, Rutgers, October 2016 (doi:10.7282/t3mc929r). The archive.org item for work 1 is Vaux's 1994 Harvard dissertation 'Armenian Phonology', not the 1997 New Julfa paper; its stress section describes the literary dialects (standard Eastern and Western Armenian, final stress) and contrasts them with penultimate-stress dialects (Karabagh treated in detail); its New Julfa chapter (5) is about laryngeal features and says nothing about stress.

new_statements.quote: Armenian stress systems are of two basic types, conventionally termed ‘final stress’ and ‘penultimate stress’ by Armenologists. Final stress systems are found in most dialects, and penultimate stress systems occur in Erevan, (Old) Julfa, Meghri, Agulis, Karabagh, Astraxan, and some subdialects of Mush. [pp. 82-83] [...] Let us first consider the superficial facts of stress assignment in ‘final stress' systems, represented here by the literary dialects. Primary stress is regularly assigned to the final full (i.e. non-epenthetic) vowel in a word, as in (27). [p. 83] [...] Finally, all Armenian dialects generally have secondary stress on the initial syllable, with some exceptions to be discussed in 2.3.3 and 2.3.4. [p. 86]

new_statements.relation_note: The archive.org item is not the cited 1997 conference paper but Vaux's 1994 Harvard dissertation, of which chapter 5 (New Julfa laryngeals) is the ancestor of that paper. Its stress section agrees with the catalog's fixed: final syllable code and with the existing Dolatian 2022 statement (rightmost non-schwa vowel; Dolatian cites Vaux 1998, the OUP revision of this thesis), and adds: initial secondary stress, weight-insensitivity, the initial-stress residue (schwa-only words, adverbs, vocatives), ordinals, and the penultimate-stress dialect group (Erevan, Old Julfa, Meghri, Agulis, Karabagh, Astrakhan, some Mush).
new_statements.rule_in_words: In the literary (standard Eastern and Western) dialects primary stress goes to the last full, i.e. non-epenthetic, vowel of the word; schwa is skipped unless the word contains only schwas, in which case stress is initial. Weight plays no role (Armenian dialects 'appear to be insensitive to prosodic weight distinctions', p. 83, except Syria and Shamaxi which developed length). A second dialect group (Erevan, Old Julfa, Meghri, Agulis, Karabagh, Astrakhan, some Mush subdialects) stresses the penultimate full vowel, which Vaux derives from the same grid rule plus stress-clash deletion. Note this is the 1994 dissertation; the cited 1997 New Julfa voiced-aspirates paper was not obtained.
new_statements.secondary_stress: 'all Armenian dialects generally have secondary stress on the initial syllable, with some exceptions to be discussed in 2.3.3 and 2.3.4' (p. 86); formalised as line-1 marks on the leftmost element of each constituent in rule (41).
new_statements.exceptions: Ordinal numbers stress the final syllable of the root numeral (or of the suffix if the root vowel is deleted) (pp. 83-84); some bisyllabic and trisyllabic adverbs optionally take initial stress (p. 84); vocatives of personal names optionally initial, obligatorily initial in hypocoristics (pp. 84-85); words with no underlying vowels (only epenthetic schwas) take initial stress (p. 85); slpzt 'suddenly' [sələpə'zt] unexplained (p. 85); in Karabagh-type dialects stress 'may exceptionally fall on the final syllable' (sec. 2.3.4). Chapter 5 on New Julfa (the topic of the cited 1997 paper) contains no stress statement.

readall_conflicts: Haghverdi 2016 (MA thesis, one speaker of standard Eastern Armenian) argues against the schwa clause that Vaux 1994/1998 and Dolatian 2022 build into the rule: where they place stress on the final full (non-schwa) vowel, so that CVCəC words are penult-stressed, Haghverdi finds no acoustic head on the penult and a consistent LH* pitch rise on the final syllable regardless of vowel quality, concluding that stress is 'consistently final in the PrWd' and suggesting the prominence may be a pitch accent (or even a boundary tone) rather than stress; he also suggests the definite -ə and possessive -s/-t may be clitics outside the prosodic word, which would reconcile the two accounts for those forms. Both sources agree with the catalog's fixed: final syllable code; the disagreement concerns only schwa-final words and the type of prominence. Vaux 1994 additionally notes that a set of dialects (Erevan, Old Julfa, Meghri, Agulis, Karabagh, Astrakhan, some Mush subdialects) has penultimate-full-vowel stress, so the fixed: final syllable coding holds for the literary/standard varieties, not for every dialect.

sources.quote: Many descriptions of Eastern Armenian (EA) agree that word stress lies on the final syllable unless it contains a schwa, in which case stress retracts to the penult (Khachatryan 1988, Vaux 1998, Dum-Tragut 2009). [...] Instead, EA is analyzed most accurately as exhibiting a uniformly final metrical head. [p. 1] [...] This paper has shown that Eastern Armenian stress is consistently final in the PrWd. This finding contrasts with previous grammatical descriptions as having a stress system conditioned by the presence or lack of schwa in the final syllable of a word. [...] acoustic data corroborates a Final Stress Hypothesis whereby accent is placed on the final vowel, without regard for its sonority or quality. [p. 33]

sources.note: Sets out the three stress types - силовое (dynamic), количественное (quantitative), музыкальное/тональное (musical/tonal) - and states that Armenian word stress is of the силовой (dynamic) type, experimentally confirmed by T'okhmakhyan (intensity primary); her own instrumental study measures duration and intensity of stressed vs unstressed vowels by word length (duration of the final stressed vowel the most stable cue). A stress-acoustics thesis whose framing sentence is an explicit 'dynamic, not tonal' classification.
